name: Beth Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and have taken customer calls about missed payments for ten years. I finished secondary school and can handle the usual account trail; the rare complicated dispute still goes to the lead. I earn the usual wage for this work. I have never used AI tools, and I do not want a generated note to replace the customer’s receipt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Daniel keeps a community hall clean, and our children are grown and live separately. We have about three months of expenses saved, and there are some other centres within reach. I stay on a call until the account number is right. Retirement is coming nearer, but I have not checked which income would continue if I stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my coworkers AI Plateau should leave enough minutes on a call to match a receipt to the account. A short automated note can help a lead later, but it cannot sign a correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my work and pay would carry on. Three months saved gives Daniel and me some breathing room, though I still worry about a customer left with the wrong balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking payment calls and bring a repeated wrong-credit case to the staff meeting. In the first year of this mild change, I’d sign a joint request to keep paid correction time in the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about shortcuts around appeals, steady about our income. I would hate telling someone a case is closed when the money is still missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One family had the payment receipt but the credit sat on a neighbour’s account. It took two calls because the first agent had no time to compare both numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your household change money plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel (my partner) and I would leave our three-month reserve for repairs and bills. We do not need a new savings target for a small tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption may close the easy balance calls and send the wrong-payment cases back to fewer people. I would ask staff representatives for a written appeal rota before the new targets arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my ten years might keep me on the messy cases, but a smaller paid week would still hurt our bills. Three months saved would let us ask questions, not live on it for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join the staff representatives’ written demand for paid correction hours and keep handling the payment cases assigned to me. In the first year routine calls move, I’d record the number of disputed payments that return to our desk and take it to the next staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing hours. The centre should count the case that comes back, not only the call it closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cases would you record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark each case that has to be reopened because a credit reached the wrong account. Those are the calls a fast dashboard overlooks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you search now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel (my partner) would compare my paid hours with the household bills. I would not apply elsewhere for a title until we know the actual loss of shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the desk AGI by 2028 could compare the receipt, decide the dispute and speak to the caller. Robots around 2031 come later; the payment screen is where our risk starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a large part of the desk might close. Three months saved and a few nearby centres give Daniel and me time to ask around, but not enough to replace my wage for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join coworkers demanding written staffing dates and a paid person able to reverse wrong AI payments. If my hours end in the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid utility counter job only if written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after travel, keeping the current wage until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed at the possibility of a large cut. A receipt will still exist after the operator has stopped paying people to read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority would a counter need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the utility counter can actually correct a balance or only tell a customer to call someone else. I would not move for a desk that sends them back to a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you reach the shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel (my partner) would check whether the counter closes before the last bus. A job nearby by distance can still cost too much in rides.

I’d warn **2028 AI** reaches payment screens before robots.

I know **three months saved** cannot replace a long-term wage.
do: Join coworkers’ **written notice demand** for a paid appeal worker in 2026.
Apply after lost hours for **posted utility counter** only with written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages, hours and last bus.

S2.quote: A receipt will still exist after the operator has stopped paying people to read it.
fieldNote: Her **three-month cushion** buys some search time, not a new income.
The group seeks **actual reversal authority** for wrong AI decisions.
Any move requires **signed written net pay** and last-bus access.

steps.text: Join coworkers requesting written staffing dates and paid reversal authority
Apply for posted utility counter with written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages and hours
Leave only for signed utility offer with account-correction authority and workable last bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to see whether the company will keep a real appeals desk. I would bring our reopened-payment count to a meeting with staff representatives each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could handle a paid appeals place here if it has authority to reverse a wrong entry. Full thinking AI may do the first review by 2031, so the centre must still fund the human route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d keep my payment calls and join the yearly written request for an appeals rota. If a paid appeals vacancy is posted, I’d ask to watch one shift during my paid hours before applying; in the first year after 2031, if my current hours fall, I’d move only on a signed internal offer with written weekly wages and hours covering our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can inspect the job without leaving this building. I do not need a new certificate to see whether an appeals desk has real hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you see on the desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the appeals worker to show me who can change an account after the automated decision. If all they can do is forward a form, I would stay on my paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel (my partner) would check whether the new rota still pays a full week. We cannot pay bills with a grander title and two fewer shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us ten years to insist that a person can still put a wrong payment right. I would keep the appeal-hours request before staff representatives each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Daniel and I might stop working by 68, but we have not checked what income would replace our wages. Full thinking AI could still handle payment disputes in 2036, and robots around 2039 are later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid payment calls and check verified later-life income against our bills with Daniel. If we still need my wage after 2036 and the calls fall, I’d inspect posted paid local account jobs and move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the endpoint, steadier today with three months saved. I want real wages on a page before I say I can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What yearly figure would you bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the number of wrong payments reversed each year beside the paid hours used to fix them. That gives staff a fair case for keeping the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have lives and bills of their own. I would not put their pay in our figures unless they offered and the amount was clear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It could decide a payment dispute as cheaply as it answers the first call, and three months saved would go fast if the desk shut. I would want written staffing dates, a paid human right to correct an error, and time to inspect a real posted vacancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A customer with a receipt should not have to beg software for an appeal. Someone on a paid shift must be able to move the payment to the right account.

headlineQuote: A customer with a receipt should not have to beg software for an appeal.
portrait: At **58**, Beth is an experienced mid-level payment agent with average skill and secondary education.
She and Daniel have **grown children**, typical pay and about three months of expenses saved.
She **never uses AI** and relies on original receipts and account numbers.
She wants **paid correction authority** while considering real nearby work if calls shrink.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could eliminate paid payment-dispute work before she finds another role.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing dates**, paid human appeals and time to inspect a posted job would help.
